Arithmetic function (f:Z>0​→C)

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Number theory
OurBigBook.com Words: 7k Articles: 72
An arithmetic function is a function whose domain of a function is the positive integers, usually taking values in the complex numbers. Thus f(1),f(2),… are its values; f(0) is outside this domain of a function. Examples include the divisor function, with τ(12)=6, and the sum-of-divisors function, with σ1​(12)=28. Studying an arithmetic function packages a question about each positive integer into one object whose values can be combined using Dirichlet convolution. [ref]

Liouville function (λ(n))

Words: 24
Arithmetic function OurBigBook.com
The Liouville function is λ(n)=(−1)Ω(n), where Ω(n) is the total number of prime factors counted with multiplicity. It is a completely multiplicative function: multiplication adds prime-factor multiplicities, so λ(ab)=λ(a)λ(b).

Summatory function (A(x)=∑n≤x​a(n))

Words: 38
Arithmetic function OurBigBook.com
The summatory function of an arithmetic function a is A(x)=∑1≤n≤x​a(n). For example, the prime-counting function sums the indicator of the prime numbers, while the divisor summatory function sums the divisor function. Grouping equal values of ⌊x/d⌋ often speeds up identities involving summatory functions.

Radical of an integer (rad(n)=∏p∣n​p)

Words: 418 Articles: 1
Arithmetic function OurBigBook.com
The radical of an integer n>0 is the product of its distinct prime factors, each included exactly once. If the prime factorization is n=p1a1​​⋯prar​​ with distinct prime numbers pi​ and positive integer exponents ai​, then
rad(n)=p1​⋯pr​=∏p∣n​p.
(1)
Thus the radical of an integer remembers which prime factors occur and forgets their prime valuations. At n=1, the empty product gives rad(1)=1. The domain of a function here is the positive integers; zero is excluded. [ref]
For example, 72=23⋅32 has distinct prime factors 2,3, so rad(72)=2⋅3=6. Similarly,
rad(30)=30,rad(32)=2,rad(36)=6,
(2)
using the prime factorizations 30=2⋅3⋅5, 32=25 and 36=22⋅32. The prime omega function counts the retained prime factors, while the total number of prime factors counts their occurrences before repetitions are removed.
The radical of an integer is its largest squarefree divisor. Indeed, a squarefree divisor chooses at most one copy of each prime factor, so it divides rad(n); the radical of an integer itself is a squarefree divisor. Consequently,
rad(n)∣n,rad(n)≤n,rad(n)=n ⟺ n is squarefree.
(3)
The last statement follows because every nonzero prime valuation is then one. It includes n=1, a squarefree integer. Applying the radical of an integer twice also changes nothing: rad(rad(n))=rad(n).
For any positive integers a,b, the exact product rule is
rad(ab)=rad(gcd(a,b))rad(a)rad(b)​.
(4)
To prove it, a prime factor dividing just one input occurs once in the numerator and not in the denominator. A prime factor dividing both occurs twice in the numerator and once in the denominator, since it divides their greatest common divisor. Each prime factor of ab therefore remains exactly once. For coprime integers, the denominator is rad(1)=1, proving the radical of an integer is a multiplicative function. It is not a completely multiplicative function: rad(4)=2=4=rad(2)2.
For a worked example with shared prime factors, take a=12 and b=18. Their greatest common divisor is 6, and ab=216=23⋅33, so
rad(216)=66⋅6​=6.
(5)
This explains why prime support of an integer is useful: questions about the presence of prime factors can discard their multiplicities. For example, the squarefree divisors of 72 are exactly the integer divisors of rad(72)=6, namely 1,2,3,6. Also gcd(m,n)=1 if and only if gcd(m,rad(n))=1, because coprimality depends only on shared prime factors.
A further characterization uses mutual divisibility of powers: for positive integers a,b,
rad(a)=rad(b)⟺there exist k,ℓ≥1 with a∣bk and b∣aℓ.
(6)
If their prime supports of an integer agree, sufficiently large k,ℓ make all the required prime valuations large enough. Conversely, these two divisibility relations force each prime factor of either input to divide the other. For 72 and 36, one can take k=2 and ℓ=1: 72∣362 and 36∣72.

Prime support of an integer (P(n)={p prime:p∣n})

Words: 47
Radical of an integer OurBigBook.com
The prime support of an integer n>0 is the finite set of its distinct prime factors. For example, P(72)=P(36)={2,3}, P(30)={2,3,5} and P(1) is the empty set. Its cardinality is the prime omega function ω(n), and the product of its elements is the radical of an integer rad(n). These are two different ways to summarize the same finite set: a count and a product.

Total number of prime factors (Ω(n))

Words: 372 Articles: 1
Arithmetic function OurBigBook.com
The total number of prime factors Ω(n) counts every occurrence of a prime factor in the prime factorization of a positive integer n. Equivalently, it adds the prime valuations:
n=p1a1​​⋯prar​​⟹Ω(n)=a1​+⋯+ar​=∑p∣n​vp​(n).
(7)
One may also write Ω(n)=∑p​vp​(n) over all prime numbers, since only finitely many prime valuations are nonzero. The empty sum gives Ω(1)=0. By contrast, the prime omega function has ω(n)=r and counts distinct prime factors. [ref]
Expanding 72=23⋅32 into 2⋅2⋅2⋅3⋅3 shows Ω(72)=3+2=5, whereas ω(72)=2 and rad(72)=6. The same calculation for the comparison examples gives
n172303236​prime factorizationempty product23⋅322⋅3⋅52522⋅32​rad(n)163026​ω(n)02312​Ω(n)05354​​
(8)
The total number of prime factors agrees for 72 and 32, although their prime supports of an integer differ. Meanwhile 72 and 36 have the same radical of an integer and prime omega function, but different values of the total number of prime factors. These examples show exactly which information each arithmetic function forgets.
The total number of prime factors is a completely additive arithmetic function:
Ω(ab)=Ω(a)+Ω(b)(a,b≥1).
(9)
The proof is that multiplication adds each prime valuation, vp​(ab)=vp​(a)+vp​(b), and summing preserves that equality. No coprimality condition is needed. For example, 12=22⋅3 and 18=2⋅32 both have total number of prime factors three; their product 216=23⋅33 has six. By comparison, the prime omega function is only an additive arithmetic function: here ω(216)=2=4=ω(12)+ω(18).
There is a useful way to see the total number of prime factors as a count of elementary building blocks: any expression of n as a product of prime numbers has exactly Ω(n) factors, by the fundamental theorem of arithmetic. Equivalently, every factorization tree for n>1 has Ω(n) leaves. Repeated prime factors increase this count without introducing new kinds of prime number. The difference is the existing excess prime-factor multiplicity:
Ω(n)−ω(n)=∑p∣n​(vp​(n)−1)≥0.
(10)
Every summand is nonnegative, so Ω(n)=ω(n) if and only if n is a squarefree integer, including n=1. In particular, a prime power pk with k≥1 has Ω(pk)=k, ω(pk)=1 and rad(pk)=p.
Historically, Hardy and Ramanujan's 1917 paper explicitly separated the prime omega function from the total number of prime factors, writing them as f(n) and F(n), respectively. Their example 23⋅32⋅5 has counts three and six. That distinction let them compare two measures of how an integer is built from prime factors. [ref]

Excess prime-factor multiplicity (Ω(n)−ω(n))

Words: 28
Total number of prime factors OurBigBook.com
The nonnegative arithmetic function Ω(n)−ω(n) counts the repeated occurrences beyond the first of each prime factor. Its expectation under uniform sampling from [N] is bounded by ∑p​1/(p(p−1))≤1, independently of N.

Additive function (number theory)

Words: 77 Articles: 3
Arithmetic function OurBigBook.com
An arithmetic function f is additive when f(mn)=f(m)+f(n) for coprime integers m,n. Equivalently, f(n)=∑pk∥n​f(pk). This concerns multiplication of integers, and differs from an additive function on a vector space.

Mean of an additive arithmetic function (Af​(x))

Words: 18
Additive function (number theory) OurBigBook.com
For an additive arithmetic function, the model mean is Af​(x)=∑pk≤x​f(pk)(1−1/p)/pk. The exact uniform expectation differs by O(x−1∑pk≤x​∣f(pk)∣).

Strongly additive arithmetic function

Words: 17
Additive function (number theory) OurBigBook.com
A strongly additive arithmetic function satisfies f(pk)=f(p) for every prime p and k≥1, so f(n)=∑p∣n​f(p). The prime omega function is an example.

Completely additive arithmetic function

Words: 16
Additive function (number theory) OurBigBook.com
A completely additive arithmetic function satisfies f(mn)=f(m)+f(n) for all positive m,n, equivalently f(pk)=kf(p). The total number of prime factors is an example.

Multiplicative function (f(1)=1,f(mn)=f(m)f(n) if gcd(m,n)=1)

Words: 1k Articles: 13
Arithmetic function OurBigBook.com
An arithmetic function f is a multiplicative function when f(1)=1 and f(mn)=f(m)f(n) for all coprime integers m,n>0, meaning their greatest common divisor is 1. The condition f(1)=1 excludes the identically zero function. This definition makes no assertion about a pair whose greatest common divisor exceeds 1. [ref]
For the divisor function, the integer divisors of 2 are 1,2, those of 3 are 1,3, and those of 6 are 1,2,3,6. Hence
τ(6)=4=τ(2)τ(3)=2⋅2.
(11)
Here 2 and 3 are coprime integers. In contrast, τ(4)=3=4=τ(2)2, because the integer divisors of 4 are 1,2,4. Thus the divisor function is a multiplicative function but not a completely multiplicative function.
The practical gain is that prime factorization reduces all values to values at prime powers. For distinct prime numbers p1​,…,pr​ and positive exponents a1​,…,ar​,
n=∏k=1r​pkak​​⟹f(n)=∏k=1r​f(pkak​​).
(12)
For instance, f(12)=f(4)f(3) since 4 and 3 are coprime integers; replacing f(4) by f(2)2 additionally requires a completely multiplicative function. The short proof repeatedly applies the defining rule to prime powers belonging to different prime numbers, which are coprime integers.

Multiplicativity of an arithmetic function

Words: 29
Multiplicative function OurBigBook.com
For an arithmetic function, multiplicativity means f(1)=1 and f(mn)=f(m)f(n) whenever m,n are positive coprime integers. It allows values of an arithmetic function to be assembled from its values on prime powers, as explained under multiplicative function.

Completely multiplicative function (f(1)=1,f(mn)=f(m)f(n) for all m,n>0)

Words: 44
Multiplicative function OurBigBook.com
An arithmetic function f is a completely multiplicative function when f(1)=1 and f(mn)=f(m)f(n) for every pair of positive integers m,n. In particular f(pa)=f(p)a for every prime number p and every nonnegative exponent a. Both the constant-one arithmetic function and the identity arithmetic function are completely multiplicative functions: 1(mn)=1=1⋅1 and id(mn)=mn=id(m)id(n). The divisor function fails this stronger condition at m=n=2.

Divisor sum (F(n)=∑d∣n​f(d))

Words: 516 Articles: 2
Multiplicative function OurBigBook.com
The divisor sum of an arithmetic function f assigns to each positive integer n the sum
F(n)=∑d∣n​f(d).
(13)
Only positive integer divisors are included, so F(1)=f(1). The weights f(d) can count the integer divisors, measure their sizes, or record other arithmetic information: the constant-one arithmetic function gives the divisor function, whereas the identity arithmetic function gives the sum-of-divisors function.
Equivalently, F=f∗1, where ∗ is Dirichlet convolution and 1 is the constant-one arithmetic function. If f is a multiplicative function, then F is a multiplicative function by Multiplicativity of Dirichlet convolution. [ref]
Here is the mechanism. For positive coprime integers m,n, every positive integer divisor of mn has a unique form ab with a∣m and b∣n; moreover, a,b are coprime integers. Thus a multiplicative function satisfies
F(mn)=∑a∣m​∑b∣n​f(a)f(b)=F(m)F(n).
(14)
At a prime power, the divisor sum becomes F(pa)=f(1)+f(p)+⋯+f(pa). This turns a calculation over many integer divisors into short local calculations at prime powers.

Sum-of-divisors function (σ1​(n))

Words: 384 Articles: 1
Divisor sum OurBigBook.com
The sum-of-divisors function adds all positive integer divisors of a positive integer, including the number itself:
σ(n)=σ1​(n)=∑d∣n​d,σ(1)=1.
(15)
It is the divisor sum of the identity arithmetic function id(n)=n, so σ=id∗1 under Dirichlet convolution. Both factors are multiplicative functions, hence so is the sum-of-divisors function. The notation σ1​ distinguishes it from other weighted divisor sums. [ref]
For a prime number p and a nonnegative exponent a, the positive integer divisors of the prime power pa are precisely 1,p,…,pa. Their finite geometric series gives
σ(pa)=1+p+⋯+pa=p−1pa+1−1​.
(16)
For example, σ(8)=1+2+4+8=15=(24−1)/(2−1). For a prime factorization n=∏k=1r​pkak​​ with distinct prime numbers pk​ and positive exponents ak​, multiplicativity gives
σ(n)=∏k=1r​(1+pk​+⋯+pkak​​)=∏k=1r​pk​−1pkak​+1​−1​.
(17)
For n=1, this is an empty product, equal to 1. [ref]
The distributive property makes the formula especially beautiful: choosing one term from each factor produces each positive integer divisor exactly once, by the fundamental theorem of arithmetic. For 12=4⋅3=22⋅3, the choices form a three-by-two grid with entries 2i3j, where 0≤i≤2 and 0≤j≤1. Adding its rows gives
σ(12)=(1+2+4)+(3+6+12)=(1+2+4)(1+3)=7⋅4=28.
(18)
The divisor function counts six cells; the sum-of-divisors function adds their six values. Once the prime factorization is known, the product formula avoids testing every candidate integer divisor. Shared prime factors require care: σ(4)=7=9=σ(2)2, so the sum-of-divisors function is not a completely multiplicative function.
Subtracting the number itself gives the proper-divisor sum s(n)=σ(n)−n. Comparing s(n) with n distinguishes perfect numbers, deficient numbers, and abundant numbers. For 6, s(6)=1+2+3=6; for 28, s(28)=1+2+4+7+14=28. Both are perfect numbers. The calculation s(8)=1+2+4=7<8 makes 8 a deficient number, while s(12)=1+2+3+4+6=16>12 makes 12 an abundant number. These comparisons turn the sizes of integer divisors into a classification of positive integers. [ref]
This connection is ancient: Euclid's Elements, Book IX, Proposition 36, constructs a perfect number by multiplying the last term of 1,2,…,2k−1 by their sum, when that sum is a prime number. In modern notation, put q=2k−1 and N=2k−1q, with k≥2 and q a prime number. The sum-of-divisors function proves the construction immediately:
σ(N)=(2k−1)(1+q)=q2k=2N.
(19)
Consequently the proper-divisor sum is s(N)=N. Taking k=2,3 produces the perfect numbers 6,28. [ref]
Proper-divisor sum (s(n)=σ(n)−n)
Words: 29
Sum-of-divisors function OurBigBook.com
The proper-divisor sum, or aliquot sum, adds the positive proper divisors:
s(n)=∑d∣nd<n​​d=σ(n)−n.
(20)
In particular s(1)=0, an empty sum. Removing n from the sum-of-divisors function is essential: σ(6)=12, but its proper-divisor sum is 6.

For multiplicative functions bounded by one, the pretentious distance up to x is defined by
D(f,g;x)2=∑p≤x​p1−ℜ(f(p)g(p)​)​.

Large Fourier coefficient criterion for pretentiousness (∣ν(t)∣≤ClogXe−D(f,nit;X)2)

Words: 87
Pretentious distance OurBigBook.com
Let X≥3, and let f be a normalized multiplicative arithmetic function supported on squarefree integers, with ∣f(p)∣≤1. Form the finite measure ν=∑n​f(n)n−1−1/logXδlogn​ using Dirac measures. Under the transform convention ν(t)=∫e−itudν(u), its Euler product is ∏p​(1+f(p)p−1−1/logX−it). Expanding its logarithmic modulus, and replacing the damped prime weights by 1/p up to X with Mertens first theorem, gives the displayed absolute bound, uniformly in real t. Hence ∣ν(t)∣≥δlogX forces D(f,nit;X)2≤log(C/δ). The distance expression still defines a nonnegative pretentious score for prime values bounded by one; its actual metric interpretation uses unit-modulus values.

Pretentious distance between one and the Möbius function (D(1,μ;X)∼2loglogX​)

Words: 43
Pretentious distance OurBigBook.com
Because μ(p)=−1, the squared pretentious distance from one to the Möbius function is twice the reciprocal-prime sum. The Mertens second theorem therefore gives D(1,μ;X)2=2loglogX+2B1​+o(1). In particular the distance diverges, illustrating that a multiplicative function can be far from the constant function even though both have unit-modulus prime values.

Prime-restriction metric for pretentious distance (D(f,g;X)2=21​∑p≤X​∣f(p)−g(p)∣2/p)

Words: 59
Pretentious distance OurBigBook.com
For unit-modulus prime values, pretentious distance is the Euclidean metric on the finite vectors (f(p)/2p​)p≤X​. On whole arithmetic functions it is only a pseudometric: it sees neither values on prime powers nor primes above the cutoff. Even for every cutoff, the functions one and μ2 have distance zero but differ on nonsquarefree integers. The norm representation proves the triangle inequality and identifies exactly the quotient on which separation holds.

Pointwise product of arithmetic functions ((f⋅g)(n)=f(n)g(n))

Words: 36
Arithmetic function OurBigBook.com
The pointwise product of arithmetic functions multiplies two arithmetic functions at the same input: (f⋅g)(n)=f(n)g(n). Thus (1⋅1)(12)=1 and (id⋅1)(12)=12, using the constant-one arithmetic function and the identity arithmetic function. These differ from the corresponding Dirichlet convolution values 6 and 28, because Dirichlet convolution sums over every positive integer divisor.

Dirichlet convolution (∗)

Words: 1k Articles: 10
Arithmetic function OurBigBook.com
The Dirichlet convolution of arithmetic functions f,g is the arithmetic function
(f∗g)(n)=∑d∣n​f(d)g(n/d)=∑a,b>0ab=n​​f(a)g(b),n>0.
(24)
In the first sum, d runs over the positive integer divisors of n; the second uses ordered pairs of positive integers whose product is n. Both sums are finite. Each pair contributes one weight from f and one from g, so Dirichlet convolution combines information attached to complementary factors. It turns a divisor sum into an operation on arithmetic functions. [ref]
For n=12 the six ordered pairs are (1,12),(2,6),(3,4),(4,3),(6,2),(12,1). The constant-one arithmetic function gives one per pair, while the identity arithmetic function weights the first factor by its size:
τσ1​​=1∗1,=id∗1,​τ(12)σ1​(12)​=1+1+1+1+1+1=6,=1+2+3+4+6+12=28.​
(25)
Here τ is the divisor function and σ1​ is the sum-of-divisors function. By comparison, the pointwise product of arithmetic functions gives (1⋅1)(12)=1 and (id⋅1)(12)=12.
Commutativity follows by swapping the two entries of every ordered pair. Associativity follows by reindexing either grouping over the same ordered tuples of three positive integers:
((f∗g)∗h)(n)=∑a,b,c>0abc=n​​f(a)g(b)h(c)=(f∗(g∗h))(n).
(26)
For example, ((1∗1)∗1)(12) counts ordered tuples of three positive integers with product 12. Distribute the two occurrences of the prime factor 2 among three entries in (22+2​)=6 ways, and the one occurrence of the prime factor 3 in (21+2​)=3 ways. These binomial coefficients are the stars and bars counts of exponent choices in the nonnegative integers; prime factorization therefore gives 6⋅3=18 such tuples. Directly, the same Dirichlet convolution is ∑d∣12​τ(d)=1+2+2+3+4+6=18.
The Identity for Dirichlet convolution is ε, and the Möbius function reverses a divisor sum because μ∗1=ε. This makes Dirichlet convolution useful both for counting factorizations and for recovering an arithmetic function from its divisor sum.

Multiplicativity of Dirichlet convolution (f,g multiplicative ⟹ f∗g multiplicative)

Words: 89
Dirichlet convolution OurBigBook.com
The Dirichlet convolution of two multiplicative functions is a multiplicative function. For positive coprime integers m,n, every positive integer divisor of mn has a unique form de with d∣m and e∣n, by prime factorization. The pairs d,e and m/d,n/e are each coprime integers, so the defining rules for the two multiplicative functions separate the sum:
(f∗g)(mn)=∑d∣m​∑e∣n​f(d)f(e)g(m/d)g(n/e)=(f∗g)(m)(f∗g)(n).
(27)
Also (f∗g)(1)=f(1)g(1)=1. This short argument proves multiplicativity of both the divisor function 1∗1 and the sum-of-divisors function id∗1. The result need not be a completely multiplicative function, even when both inputs are: 1∗1=τ fails at 2⋅2. [ref]

Constant-one arithmetic function (1)

Words: 45
Dirichlet convolution OurBigBook.com
The constant-one arithmetic function has 1(n)=1 for every positive integer n, including 1(1)=1(12)=1. It is a completely multiplicative function. Its Dirichlet convolution with an arithmetic function f is the divisor sum (1∗f)(n)=∑d∣n​f(d). Thus 1∗1=τ, the divisor function. Its pointwise product of arithmetic functions with f is f itself; its Dirichlet convolution with f generally is not. The Identity for Dirichlet convolution is instead ε.

Identity arithmetic function (id)

Words: 43
Dirichlet convolution OurBigBook.com
The identity arithmetic function is id(n)=n on the positive integers, for example id(1)=1 and id(12)=12. It is a completely multiplicative function and gives the sum-of-divisors function through id∗1=σ1​ under Dirichlet convolution. It is distinct from the Identity for Dirichlet convolution ε. The identity id=1∗φ, where φ is Euler's totient function, is equivalent to ∑d∣n​φ(d)=n.

Identity for Dirichlet convolution (ε)

The Dirichlet hyperbola method turns a long summation over a Dirichlet convolution into two short ones by covering the lattice points below a hyperbola with two overlapping strips. Its simplest application is an exact count: for a positive integer N, every positive integer divisor a of n≤N corresponds to the ordered pair (a,n/a). Thus the divisor summatory function counts precisely the ordered pairs of positive integers with ab≤N:

(31)
Here τ is the divisor function, and the floor function gives the number of allowed values of b for each a. The axes are excluded, while points on ab=N are included.
Set r=⌊N​⌋, using the floor function and the positive square root. Every counted pair has a≤r or b≤r. Otherwise ab≥(r+1)2>N. The first strip contains ∑a=1r​⌊N/a⌋ points; swapping the two coordinates gives the same count for the second. Their overlap contains all r2 pairs with 1≤a,b≤r, since r2≤N. The inclusion-exclusion principle therefore gives the exact identity
D(N)=2a=1∑r​⌊aN​⌋−r2,r=⌊N​⌋.​

The subtraction is for the whole overlap square, rather than only the diagonal. The same Dirichlet hyperbola method identity holds for real x≥1, with D(x)=∑n≤x​τ(n) and r=⌊x​⌋. [ref]

Asymmetric Dirichlet hyperbola split (AB=N)

Words: 256
Dirichlet hyperbola method OurBigBook.com
A balanced Dirichlet hyperbola method split takes real thresholds A=B=N​. An asymmetric split takes 1≤A≤N and B=N/A. Every lattice point with ab≤N then has a≤A or b≤B, and every point in their overlap rectangle is allowed because AB=N. For arithmetic functions f,g, define their partial sums by F(t)=∑a≤t​f(a) and G(t)=∑b≤t​g(b), always over positive integers. The same inclusion-exclusion principle, now with weight f(a)g(b), yields
∑n≤N​(f∗g)(n)=∑a≤A​f(a)G(N/a)+∑b≤B​g(b)F(N/b)−F(A)G(B),AB=N.
(36)
No multiplicativity assumption is needed: this is a finite rearrangement of Dirichlet convolution. The constant-one arithmetic function in both positions recovers the divisor summatory function. For N=12, A=2, B=6 gives
D(12)=(12+6)+(12+6+4+3+2+2)−2⋅6=18+29−12=35.
(37)
It uses two columns and six rows, with a twelve-point overlap.
For general positive real thresholds, AB≥N is sufficient for coverage, since a>A and b>B would imply ab>AB≥N. If AB>N, however, the overlap can include points above the hyperbola. The correct subtraction is then ∑a≤A, b≤B, ab≤N​f(a)g(b); the product F(A)G(B) is justified only when the whole integer rectangle lies below it. For example, N=12, A=B=4 covers every allowed pair, but its rectangle contains the forbidden pair (4,4), so subtracting all sixteen points would give 34 instead of 35.
Conversely, the balanced integer thresholds r,r have r2≤N and still cover every allowed pair because (r+1)2>N. More generally, positive integer thresholds U,V give coverage exactly when (U+1)(V+1)>N, and their overlap is a full rectangle exactly when UV≤N. These discrete conditions explain why the square-root identity works even when r2<N.

Arithmetic work of the Dirichlet hyperbola method

Words: 186
Dirichlet hyperbola method OurBigBook.com
The direct divisor summatory function formula evaluates N floor divisions. Its balanced Dirichlet hyperbola method formula evaluates r=⌊N​⌋ floor divisions and reuses their sum for the other strip, followed by doubling and square-overlap subtraction. Thus it uses O(N​) arithmetic operations, with big O notation, in a model that counts each division, addition and multiplication as one operation. At N=106, the division counts for these two formulas are 106 and 103.
For a general Dirichlet convolution, the asymmetric formula has ⌊A⌋+⌊B⌋ outer terms; evaluating F and G has an additional cost. Under AB=N, equal thresholds minimize A+B, but an asymmetric split can be useful if the two partial sums have different evaluation costs. The balanced divisor summatory function gains the further reuse because its two arithmetic functions are identical.
These are arithmetic operation counts, rather than counts of elementary operations on binary digits: the integers grow with N, and division of longer integers costs more in that model of computational complexity theory. Computing r also requires an exact integer square root, or checking and correcting a numerical square root until r2≤N<(r+1)2 holds.

For 12=22⋅3, choose i∈{0,1,2} and j∈{0,1} to obtain 2i3j. The six values are 1,2,4,3,6,12; sorted, the positive integer divisors are 1,2,3,4,6,12. Therefore τ(12)=(2+1)(1+1)=6. The diagram makes the independent exponent choices visible.
This count is useful because a known prime factorization gives τ(n) without testing every smaller positive integer for divisibility. It also proves the divisor function is a multiplicative function: coprime integers have disjoint prime factors, so their exponent choices combine. For example τ(6)=4=τ(2)τ(3), but τ(4)=3=4=τ(2)2, so it is not a completely multiplicative function. Equivalently, τ=1∗1 under Dirichlet convolution, counting ordered pairs of positive integers whose product is n.

Arithmetic function OurBigBook.com
The Von Mangoldt function assigns a natural logarithm weight to each positive power of a prime number. For a positive integer n,
Λ(n)={logp,0,​n=pk,p prime, k≥1,otherwise.​
(40)
Here and throughout the Chebyshev functions, log means the natural logarithm. In particular, Λ(1)=0: the exponent must be positive, even though the convention in prime power allows exponent zero. The support of a function of Λ therefore consists precisely of the prime powers greater than one. [ref]
For example, Λ(2)=Λ(4)=Λ(8)=log2 and Λ(3)=Λ(9)=log3, whereas Λ(6)=Λ(12)=0. A composite number can have a nonzero weight: 8 has just one distinct prime factor. But 12=22⋅3 has two distinct prime factors, so its weight is zero. At pk the weight is logp, not log(pk)=klogp. This choice lets successive powers record successive copies of the same prime factor in the Von Mangoldt divisor identity.
The Von Mangoldt function is useful because it connects two views of the prime numbers: the prime factorization of an individual integer, through a divisor sum, and the accumulated weights below a cutoff, through the Second Chebyshev function. The latter turns questions about the distribution of prime numbers into questions about a partial sum of an arithmetic function.

At n=1 there are no prime factors, so the empty sum gives ω(1)=0. The total number of prime factors instead gives Ω(n)=∑i​ai​. [ref]
For 72=23⋅32, the prime support of an integer is {2,3} and ω(72)=2. The comparison examples give ω(30)=3, ω(32)=1 and ω(36)=2. Raising an existing prime factor to a higher power does not affect the prime omega function: ω(pk)=1 for a prime number p and k≥1. Thus the prime omega function is a strongly additive arithmetic function, with
ω(ab)=ω(a)+ω(b)if gcd(a,b)=1.
(60)
The reason is that coprime integers have disjoint prime supports of an integer. For arbitrary positive integers, their prime support of an integer combines by set union, and the shared prime factors are exactly those of the greatest common divisor. Counting this set union gives the more general identity
ω(ab)=ω(a)+ω(b)−ω(gcd(a,b)).
(61)
For a=12, b=18, both prime supports of an integer are {2,3} and gcd(a,b)=6, so ω(216)=2+2−2=2. In particular ω(4)=1=2=ω(2)+ω(2): the prime omega function is not a completely additive arithmetic function.
The prime omega function is useful for counting choices involving distinct prime factors. Every squarefree divisor of n chooses a subset of its prime support of an integer, so there are 2ω(n) squarefree divisors. For 72, this gives 22=4, namely 1,2,3,6. Also ω(rad(n))=ω(n), because the radical of an integer keeps exactly that prime support of an integer. The total number of prime factors records what this count discards, and the two counts agree exactly on squarefree integers.

Three to the distinct-prime-factor count (3ω(n))

Words: 98 Articles: 2
Prime omega function OurBigBook.com
The multiplicative arithmetic function f(n)=3ω(n) counts assignments of three labels to each distinct prime factor. It also counts pairs of squarefree divisors whose least common multiple is the radical of an integer n.

The Euler product and Mertens second theorem give ∑n≤D​3ω(n)/n≪log3D. The log-weighted convolution bound for three to the prime omega, with the Chebyshev estimate ψ(y)≪y, then gives ∑D​≤n≤D​3ω(n)≪Dlog2D. A direct bound for the full range follows from 3ω(n)≤τ3​(n), where τ3​(n)=#{(a,b,c):abc=n}:
∑n≤D​3ω(n)≤∑abc≤D​1≤D∑a≤D​a1​∑b≤D​b1​≪Dlog2D.

Log-weighted convolution bound for three to the prime omega

Three to the distinct-prime-factor count OurBigBook.com
For f(n)=3ω(n),
f(n)logn≤3(f∗Λ)(n).
(63)
If pa∥n, its contribution to (f∗Λ)(n) is f(n)(a−1+1/3)logp. Since 3(a−1+1/3)≥a, summing over the prime factors proves the bound. Here ∗ is Dirichlet convolution and Λ is the Von Mangoldt function.

Möbius function (μ(n))

Words: 896 Articles: 7
Arithmetic function OurBigBook.com
The Möbius function assigns a cancellation weight to each positive integer:
μ(n)=⎩⎨⎧​1(−1)r0​n=1,n=p1​⋯pr​ with distinct primes p1​,…,pr​,p2∣n for some prime p.​
(64)
Thus a squarefree integer contributes a sign determined by its number of distinct prime factors; a repeated prime factor makes the weight zero. This packages the alternating signs of inclusion-exclusion into an arithmetic function. [ref]
For example, μ(2)=μ(3)=−1, μ(6)=1, and μ(30)=(−1)3=−1, since 30=2⋅3⋅5. In contrast, μ(4)=μ(12)=μ(60)=0: all three have the square of the prime number 2 as a divisor. On prime powers, μ(p)=−1 and μ(pa)=0 for a≥2.
The Möbius function is a multiplicative function: for coprime integers, their prime factors are disjoint, so either a squared prime factor forces both sides of μ(mn)=μ(m)μ(n) to vanish, or the counts of distinct prime factors add and their signs multiply. It is not a completely multiplicative function, since μ(4)=0=1=μ(2)2. Its Möbius divisor-sum identity makes it the inverse of the constant-one arithmetic function under Dirichlet convolution: μ∗1=ε, the Identity for Dirichlet convolution. This is why the small set of weights −1,0,1 can undo an entire divisor sum.

Möbius divisor-sum identity (∑d∣n​μ(d)=1n=1​)

Words: 177
Möbius function OurBigBook.com
For every positive integer n, the divisor sum of the Möbius function is
∑d∣n​μ(d)={10​n=1,n>1.​
(65)
The sum includes all positive integer divisors, but only squarefree divisors contribute. Equivalently, μ∗1=ε under Dirichlet convolution, where 1 is the constant-one arithmetic function and ε is the Identity for Dirichlet convolution. [ref]
Each squarefree divisor chooses a subset of the distinct prime factors of n, contributing (−1)r when that subset has r elements. Expanding a product therefore gives
∑d∣n​μ(d)=∏p∣n​(1−1).
(66)
For n>1 at least one prime factor occurs, so the product is zero. At n=1 it is an empty product, equal to one. This is the same alternating cancellation that drives inclusion-exclusion.
For 30=2⋅3⋅5, all eight positive integer divisors are squarefree integers, giving
μ(1)+μ(2)+μ(3)+μ(5)+μ(6)+μ(10)+μ(15)+μ(30)=1−1−1−1+1+1+1−1=0.
(67)
Pair each subset not containing 2 with the subset obtained by inserting 2: (1,2),(3,6),(5,10),(15,30). Each pair cancels. The same nonzero terms occur for 60, because its squarefree divisors are still the integer divisors of 30; its other integer divisors have Möbius function value zero.
The Möbius divisor-sum identity is the cancellation behind Möbius inversion and reciprocal Dirichlet series: aggregation over integer divisors has an exact inverse.

Möbius harmonic logarithmic moments (Aj​(x))

Words: 68
Möbius function OurBigBook.com
Put Aj​(x)=∑d≤x​μ(d)logj(x/d)/d. The elementary estimates are
A0​(x)=O(1),A1​(x)=O(1),A2​(x)=2logx+O(1).
(68)
The identities ∑d​μ(d)⌊x/d⌋=1 and ∑d​μ(d)H⌊x/d⌋​/d=1 give the first two bounds. Convolve the harmonic divisor sum with μ(d)/d: because μ∗τ=1, its left side is H⌊x⌋​. Thus 21​A2​+2γA1​+cA0​=logx+O(1). The summed error is O(x−1/2∑d≤x​d−1/2log(2x/d))=O(1).
This elementary smoothing argument is used in Selberg's original proof and Ramaré's sieve lectures, Lemma 4.2.

Möbius inversion formula (g=f∗1⟺f=μ∗g)

Words: 323
Möbius function OurBigBook.com
Möbius inversion recovers an arithmetic function from its divisor sum. For arithmetic functions f,g, the following statements are equivalent, with each equality required for every positive integer n:
g(n)=∑d∣n​f(d)⟺f(n)=∑d∣n​μ(d)g(n/d).
(69)
Here d ranges over positive integer divisors of n and μ is the Möbius function. No multiplicativity assumption is needed, and both sums are finite. The right side can also be written ∑d∣n​μ(n/d)g(d) by exchanging complementary integer divisors. [ref]
The divisor sum g(n) bundles f(n) together with values at smaller integer divisors. Möbius inversion subtracts aggregates indexed by one distinct prime factor, adds those indexed by two, and continues with the alternating signs of inclusion-exclusion. A divisor containing a squared prime factor receives weight zero. The Möbius divisor-sum identity ensures that every unwanted contribution cancels exactly.
In Dirichlet convolution notation, g=f∗1 and μ∗1=ε, where 1 is the constant-one arithmetic function and ε is the Identity for Dirichlet convolution. Associativity and commutativity give the short proof:
μ∗g=μ∗(1∗f)=(μ∗1)∗f=ε∗f=f.
(70)
Convolving f=μ∗g with 1 proves the reverse implication. At n=1, the formula reduces to f(1)=g(1) because μ(1)=1.
For a worked example, take f(n)=φ(n), Euler's totient function. The totient divisor-sum identity says that g(n)=n, the identity arithmetic function:
g(12)=φ(1)+φ(2)+φ(3)+φ(4)+φ(6)+φ(12)=1+1+2+2+2+4=12.
(71)
This identity comes from classifying the integers 1,…,n by their greatest common divisor with n: the group with gcd(j,n)=h has φ(n/h) members, since j/h and n/h are coprime integers. Summing the group sizes gives n, as detailed under totient divisor-sum identity.
Now undo this aggregation with the Möbius function:
φ(12)​=μ(1)12+μ(2)6+μ(3)4+μ(4)3+μ(6)2+μ(12)1=12−6−4+0+2+0=4.​
(72)
The nonzero terms use d=1,2,3,6; d=4,12 vanish because they contain the square of the prime number 2. The four surviving integers coprime to 12 are 1,5,7,11.
This example also reveals why Möbius inversion is useful: it turns an easy count of all objects into a count satisfying a coprimality restriction. Expanding over subsets of distinct prime factors gives
φ(n)=∑d∣n​μ(d)dn​=n∏p∣n​(1−p1​).
(73)
The product is inclusion-exclusion over multiples of the prime factors. For 12, it gives 12(1−1/2)(1−1/3)=4. More generally, whenever a counting problem produces a divisor sum, Möbius inversion lets that aggregate be reversed without solving a new system of equations.

Prime number asymptotic from Mertens cancellation (M(x)=o(x)⟹ψ(x)=x+o(x))

Words: 69
Mertens function OurBigBook.com
Let Δ(N)=∑n≤N​(τ(n)−logn−2γ). The Möbius divisor-sum identity and the Von Mangoldt divisor identity give μ∗τ=1 and μ∗log=Λ, so
ψ(N)=N−2γ−∑d≤N​μ(d)Δ(⌊N/d⌋).
(75)
Here ∗ is Dirichlet convolution. The divisor summatory asymptotic bounds the terms with d≤N/K in absolute value by O(N/K​). For d>N/K, group by j=⌊N/d⌋<K: the remaining sum is ∑j<K​Δ(j)(M(N/j)−M(N/(j+1)))=oK​(N). First let N tend to infinity, then K tend to infinity. This proves the Second Chebyshev function asymptotic from cancellation of the Mertens function.

Mertens bound from a log-integrable Chebyshev error (M(x)≪x/logx)

Words: 64
Mertens function OurBigBook.com
Suppose Ψ(x)=x+O(xE(x)) and ∑j≥0​sup2j≤u<2j+1​∣E(u)∣<∞. The Möbius divisor-sum identity gives ∑d≤x​μ(d)/d=O(1). The exact Dirichlet convolution identity μlog=−μ∗Λ then gives ∑n≤x​μ(n)logn=O(x), because its error is a convergent dyadic harmonic sum. Since ∑n≤x​log(x/n)=O(x), the displayed Mertens function bound follows. The classical Prime number theorem error E(x)=e−clogx​ meets the summability condition. This is a deduction from the Chebyshev error itself, without a separate estimate for the reciprocal zeta function.
